content: It may take several weeks to extract the appropriate data for analysis. Electronic-based data systems generally require less time to complete checklists compared to paper-based systems. Time should also be allocated to summarize the findings of the checklist before dissemination. A Basic Management Unit (BMU) is defined by its responsibilities in management, supervision, and monitoring. A BMU for tuberculosis (TB) control may include multiple treatment facilities, one or more laboratories, and one or more hospitals. The defining characteristic of a BMU is the presence of a manager or coordinator who oversees TB control activities within the unit. This individual maintains a master register of all TB patients under treatment, which is used to monitor the program and report indicators to higher administrative levels. Typically, BMUs correspond to a government’s second sub-national administrative division, such as a district or county. International guidelines recommend that a BMU should cover a population of 50,000 to 150,000 people, or up to 300,000 in large cities. Before completing the checklist for TB surveillance and vital registration systems, it is essential to characterize the national TB surveillance system. This includes answering specific questions about the system's structure, data collection methods, and reporting processes. Data in TB diagnostic units, health centers, and clinics may be recorded electronically on national, state/provincial, or local internet-based systems, or on paper. It is important to determine whether all service delivery points systematically use standardized TB data collection forms and tools. Additionally, the scope of TB cases included in the national surveillance data should be clarified, such as whether cases from non-NTP providers, prisons, or private practitioners are included. The types of TB data available at the national level should be identified, such as summaries for groups of cases. The expected frequency of data transmission from the first sub-national administrative level to the national level should also be established, whether it is real-time, monthly, quarterly, or less frequent. Furthermore, the levels at which TB data are systematically verified for accuracy, timeliness, and completeness should be specified. Quality assurance procedures for TB data should be systematically undertaken. These may include quality controls for electronic surveillance systems, supervisory monitoring visits to service units and sub-national levels, and other specified methods. Feedback on TB data quality should be systematically provided to all lower reporting levels. National TB case data for a given calendar year should be considered ready for national analyses and reporting by a specific time, such as before April, May, or June of the following year. Documentation or instructions for data collection and reporting should be available, such as training materials or online resources. The national TB program should have a training plan that includes staff involved in data collection and reporting at all levels of the reporting process. The number of staff working on TB surveillance at the national level should be identified, including full-time and part-time epidemiologists, statisticians, data managers, and data quality officers. It should also be determined whether a national TB surveillance report is routinely produced and disseminated annually, and whether there are written goals for the surveillance system. A long-term financial plan and budget should be in place to support TB surveillance activities. The last evaluation of the TB surveillance system should be noted, whether it occurred within the past five years, five to ten years, or never. Case definitions for TB should be consistent with WHO guidelines. Laboratory-confirmed cases should be distinguished from clinically diagnosed cases, new cases from previously treated cases, and pulmonary cases from extrapulmonary cases. Surveillance systems should be designed to capture a minimum set of variables for all reported TB cases, including age, sex, year of registration, bacteriological results, history of previous treatment, anatomical site of disease, and patient identifiers for case-based systems. Surveillance data should provide direct measures of drug-resistant TB in new cases, with rifampicin susceptibility status documented for at least 75% of new pulmonary TB cases or through a nationally representative drug resistance survey. Similarly, surveillance data should provide direct measures of HIV prevalence in TB cases, with HIV status documented for at least 80% of all notified TB cases or through a representative sample in settings with low-level HIV epidemics. Data in quarterly reports should be accurate, complete, and internally consistent. Sub-totals of TB cases by age group, sex, and case type should match the total number of reported TB cases in at least 95% of quarterly reports. Data for a minimum set of variables should be available for at least 95% of reported TB cases in BMU TB registers. TB surveillance data should be internally consistent over time. If vital registration data are available, they should align with TB surveillance data. Benchmarks include the ratio of pulmonary to extrapulmonary TB cases, the ratio of male to female TB cases, the proportion of childhood TB cases, year-to-year changes in case notification rates, and the ratio of presumptive TB cases to total TB notifications. The population should have good access to healthcare, with benchmarks such as an under-five mortality rate below 10 per 1,000 live births and less than 25% of total health expenditure being out-of-pocket. The vital registration system should have high national coverage and quality, with causes of death documented for at least 90% of recorded deaths and less than 10% of deaths assigned ill-defined ICD codes. The TB surveillance system should be evaluated using methods such as the Service Availability and Readiness Assessment (SARA), which involves health facility visits, key informant interviews, and observation of key items. Data quality modules for TB should be included in such assessments to ensure the system meets established standards.
